claim: Ten healthy, right-handed volunteers (age range: 21–27 years, 6 females) participated in the study.
source: Ten healthy, right-handed volunteers (age range: 21–27 years, 6 females) took part in the study, and were paid £10/hr for their time.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant demographics in the methods section.

claim: Each participant completed two experimental sessions, approximately 1 week apart.
source: Each participant completed two experimental sessions, approximately 1 week apart, with each lasting approximately 2 hr (of which approximately 1 hr was spent on performing the task).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design in the methods section.

claim: Each participant viewed a total of 7680 stimuli across two sessions.
source: Over two sessions, each observer viewed a total of 7680 stimuli to maximize the statistical power of within-participant pattern analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of trials in the methods section.

claim: Observers correctly detected approximately 70% of targets.
source: On average, observers correctly detected approximately 70% of targets (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral performance, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Observers made approximately 50% false alarms to near targets with offsets of ± 11.25º from the target angle.
source: They also made a large proportion of false alarms to near targets (approximately 50% for offsets from the target angle of ± 11.25º), with false alarms rapidly dropping for more distant non-targets.
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral performance in the results section.

claim: Reaction times were distributed around 550 ms.
source: Reaction times were distributed around 550 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), with no strong effect of target proximity on reaction time (p > 0.35, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about reaction time data, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Target proximity did not affect reaction time (F3,27 = 1.036, p = 0.393).
source: Reaction times were distributed around 550 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), with no strong effect of target proximity on reaction time (p > 0.35, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical test of reaction time differences, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stimulus orientation was represented in MEG/EEG signals from 52–500 ms relative to stimulus onset (cluster-corrected p = 0.0019).
source: Stimulus tuning curves showed that MEG/EEG signals (EEG sensors were added to the analysis in combined MEG/EEG sessions) reflected stimulus orientation shortly after its onset (Figure 2B, Figure 3B,C, Figure 3A, 52–500 ms relative to stimulus onset, cluster-corrected p = 0.0019).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing and significance of stimulus decoding, supported by Figures 2B and 3A.

claim: Template orientation information was present in the MEG/EEG signal during stimulus processing from –72 to 324 ms (cluster p = 0.0045).
source: Template orientation information was also present in the MEG/EEG signal during stimulus processing (Figure 3C, –72 to 324 ms, cluster p = 0.0045).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing and significance of template decoding, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Template coding began significantly earlier than stimulus coding (template: –72 ± 13 ms, stimulus: 52 ± 6 ms, t9 = –8.61, p = 3*10–6).
source: A jack-knife analysis comparing onset latencies between template and stimulus coding showed that template coding began significantly earlier (template: –72 ± 13 ms, stimulus: 52 ± 6 ms, t9 = –8.61, p = 3*10–6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical comparison of onset latencies.

claim: A strong effect of angular distance emerged around 200 ms (164–596 ms, cluster p = 0.0024).
source: A strong effect of angular distance emerged around 200 ms (Figure 3E, 164–596 ms, cluster p = 0.0024, with an onset that was significantly later than for the stimulus orientation, t9 = 3.25, p = 0.002).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing and significance of angular distance decoding, supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Angular distance onset was significantly later than stimulus orientation onset (t9 = 3.25, p = 0.002).
source: A strong effect of angular distance emerged around 200 ms (Figure 3E, 164–596 ms, cluster p = 0.0024, with an onset that was significantly later than for the stimulus orientation, t9 = 3.25, p = 0.002).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical comparison of onset latencies.

claim: Angular distance effect was present when training only on trials without a response (172–596 ms, cluster p = 0.0014).
source: This effect was also present when training only on trials without a response (172–596 ms, cluster p = 0.0014), which discounts the possibility that this analysis simply reflected the difference in neural signals between responded trials (which were most frequent for small angular distances) and non-responded trials (most frequent for large angular distances).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a control analysis to rule out motor-related confounds.

claim: All three task variables (stimulus, template, and angular distance) were encoded in signals in visuo-parietal sensors.
source: To a first approximation, all three variables were encoded in signals in visuo-parietal sensors (Figure 3B,D,F).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the topographic distribution of decoding, supported by Figure 3B, D, and F.

claim: Stimulus orientation decoding was significant in one main cluster along the diagonal (64–544 ms in training time, 52–436 ms in test time, cluster p = 0.0024).
source: Stimulus orientation decoding was significant in one main cluster along the diagonal (64–544 ms in training time, 52–436 ms in test time, cluster p = 0.0024, significant cluster extent indicated by color saturation in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cross-temporal decoding results, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Stimulus decoding was time-specific, with decoding dropping at off-diagonal train-test time points.
source: More importantly, stimulus decoding was time-specific, with decoding dropping at off-diagonal train-test time points.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dynamic nature of stimulus coding.

claim: Off-diagonal generalization for stimulus decoding was significantly lower in a cluster from 52–304 ms (training time) and from 88–436 ms (generalization time, cluster p = 0.0031).
source: Off-diagonal generalization was significantly lower in a cluster (black outline in Figure 4A) stretching from 52–304 ms (training time) and from 88–436 ms (generalization time, cluster p = 0.0031, based on cluster extent, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical test for dynamic coding, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Template information was present in an early cluster (training time: −140–340 ms, test time: −140–316 ms, relative to stimulus onset, cluster p = 0.0191).
source: Template information (Figure 4B) was present in an early cluster (training time: −140–340 ms, test time: −140–316 ms, relative to stimulus onset, cluster p = 0.0191).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cross-temporal template decoding, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Template decoding showed no significant attenuation of decoding on the off-diagonal.
source: In contrast to the stimulus decoding, template decoding showed no significant attenuation of decoding on the off-diagonal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal stability of template coding.

claim: Decision-relevant angular-distance decoding showed strongest decoding along the diagonal (training time: 4–592 ms, test time: 64–592 ms, cluster p = 0.0009).
source: Nevertheless, the strongest decoding was along the diagonal (training time: 4–592 ms, test time: 64–592 ms, cluster p = 0.0009), with significantly reduced off-diagonal generalization in this time window (training time 316–424 ms, generalization time 472–592 ms, cluster p = 0.008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cross-temporal angular distance decoding.

claim: Off-diagonal generalization for angular distance was significantly reduced (training time 316–424 ms, generalization time 472–592 ms, cluster p = 0.008).
source: Nevertheless, the strongest decoding was along the diagonal (training time: 4–592 ms, test time: 64–592 ms, cluster p = 0.0009), with significantly reduced off-diagonal generalization in this time window (training time 316–424 ms, generalization time 472–592 ms, cluster p = 0.008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dynamic nature of angular distance coding.

claim: Training template weights on template orientations around stimulus onset (–150 to +300 ms) showed a strong trend toward generalizing to stimulus decoding shortly after onset (52–124 ms, corr. p = 0.063).
source: Training the population tuning-curve weights on template orientations around the time of stimulus onset (–150 to +300 ms) showed a strong trend toward generalizing to stimulus decoding shortly after onset (Figure 5A, 52–124 ms, corr. p = 0.063).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cross-generalization between template and stimulus patterns, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Using only the pre-stimulus time window (–150 to 0 ms) to train the template pattern, stimulus information could be extracted in the immediate post-stimulus period (average over 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, t9 = 2.45, p = 0.037).
source: Using only the pre-stimulus time window (–150 to 0 ms) to train the template pattern, stimulus information could still be extracted in this immediate post-stimulus period (Figure 5B, average over 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, t9 = 2.45, p = 0.037), indicating that template-specific neural patterns may be pre-activated immediately before stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about pre-activation of template patterns, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Template activity patterns and stimulus activity patterns cross-generalize only transiently.
source: This result indicates that template activity patterns and stimulus activity patterns do cross-generalize (e.g., Stokes et al., 2009), but only transiently.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal characteristics of cross-generalization, with citation to prior work.

claim: Template- and stimulus-discriminative patterns correspond only in the earliest encoding period, but not later.
source: The template- and the stimulus-discriminative patterns correspond only in the earliest encoding period, but not later (even though stimulus decoding itself persisted up to 500 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal specificity of pattern correspondence.

claim: The representational similarity of stimulus orientations remained much more stationary than the discriminative patterns, with a significant cluster from 28–596 ms (cluster p = 0.005).
source: In contrast to the dynamically varying stimulus-discriminative patterns, the representational similarity remained much more stationary (Figure 6A), with a stable plateau of high correlations (Fisher-transformed Pearson's rho) from the earliest time of stimulus decoding. We found a significant (on- and off-diagonal) cluster early in the epoch (28–596 ms, cluster p = 0.005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about representational similarity analysis results, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: One short-lived dynamic cluster emerged in stimulus RSA (training time 82–146 ms, generalization time 130–226 ms, cluster p=0.0075).
source: While one short-lived dynamic cluster emerged (training time 82–146 ms, generalization time 130–226 ms, cluster p=0.0075, see black outline in Figure 6A), the majority of the epoch was dominated by time-stable correlations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a brief period of dynamic coding in the RSA, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: The representational similarity of angular distance was stable throughout the trial, with dissimilarity matrices correlating significantly in a later window (172–588 ms, cluster p = 0.0026).
source: Similarly, the representational similarity of angular distance was stable throughout the trial (Figure 6B). Dissimilarity matrices correlated significantly in a later window in the trial (172–588 ms, cluster p = 0.0026), with no time points where within-time correlations were significantly higher than between-time correlations (all p > 0.20).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal stability of angular distance representation, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: The template-sorted dissimilarity matrix correlated significantly with the stimulus-sorted dissimilarity around the time of visual processing (cluster from –48 to 196 ms for template, 88–208 ms for stimulus, cluster p = 0.038).
source: The template-sorted dissimilarity matrix correlated significantly with the stimulus-sorted dissimilarity around the time of visual processing (cluster in Figure 7A, template structure from –48 to 196 ms, stimulus structure from 88–208 ms, cluster p = 0.038).
evidence: This is a direct statement about cross-generalization of representational structure between template and stimulus, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: The within-time comparison between templates and stimuli showed a significant correlation from 104–176 ms (p = 0.036).
source: The within-time comparison between templates and stimuli (i.e., the values along the diagonal) also showed a significant correlation (Figure 7B, 104–176 ms, p = 0.036, with trends toward significance between 412–464 ms, p = 0.079, and 552–596 ms, p = 0.086).
evidence: This is a direct statement about within-time representational similarity, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: During the stimulus-encoding period (50–250 ms after stimulus onset), conditions fell onto a well-ordered circle in the MDS projection.
source: During the stimulus-encoding period (50–250 ms after stimulus onset), conditions fell onto a well-ordered circle: topographies were more similar (had a smaller Mahalanobis distance) if they were evoked by more similar stimulus orientations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the circular geometry of stimulus representation, with reference to MDS visualization.

claim: The circular geometry was not present in the data before the onset of stimulus processing (–50 to +50 ms relative to stimulus onset).
source: This geometry was not present in the data before the onset of stimulus processing (–50 to +50 ms relative to stimulus onset, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the absence of circular structure before stimulus onset, supported by Figure 7C.

claim: The stimulus similarity matrix significantly fit the neural data from 44–432 ms (cluster p = 0.002).
source: The stimulus similarity matrix significantly fit the neural data (Figure 7E, 44–432 ms, cluster p = 0.002).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the fit of circular geometry to stimulus data, supported by Figure 7E.

claim: The neural dissimilarity matrix between different template orientations was well described by the same simplex structure (48–300 ms, cluster p = 0.0012).
source: Likewise, the neural dissimilarity matrix between different template orientations was well described by the same simplex structure (Figure 7G,H, 48–300 ms, cluster p = 0.0012, with a second cluster around the time of the next stimulus).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the circular geometry of template representation, supported by Figure 7G and H.

claim: Mean projections along the task-irrelevant axis for conditions with equal magnitude but different sign diverged around the time of decision formation (348–588 ms, corrected p = 0.004).
source: Mean projections along the task-irrelevant axis for conditions with equal magnitude but different sign diverged around the time of decision formation (348–588 ms, corrected p = 0.004, Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the encoding of task-irrelevant signed differences, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: Biased competition provides a broad framework for how the brain interprets new sensory information in light of the current search template.
source: Biased competition (Desimone and Duncan, 1995) provides a broad framework for how the brain interprets new sensory information in light of the current search template.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior theoretical work.

claim: A central tenet of biased competition is that attention tonically pre-activates visual cortical neurons with receptive fields for relevant, template-matching stimuli.
source: A central tenet is that attention tonically pre-activates visual cortical neurons with receptive fields for relevant, template-matching stimuli (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Chelazzi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the biased competition model, citing prior work.

claim: Single-cell neurophysiology and human fMRI have demonstrated that template representation and stimulus processing can occur in overlapping neural populations in the visual cortex.
source: Single-cell neurophysiology (Chelazzi et al., 1993; Luck et al., 1997; Chelazzi et al., 1998) and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI; Chawla et al., 1999; Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000; Silver et al., 2007; Kastner et al., 2009; Reddy et al., 2009) have demonstrated that template representation and stimulus processing can occur in overlapping neural populations in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing multiple prior studies.

claim: Stimulus and template activity patterns cross-generalize when measured with fMRI, implying that the two share a common neural code.
source: Moreover, stimulus and template activity patterns cross-generalize (when measured with fMRI, Stokes et al., 2009), implying that the two share a common neural code.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior fMRI work.

claim: Population-level analyses of time-resolved neural recordings show that stimulus decoding is highly time-specific, with discriminative activity patterns changing at the millisecond scale.
source: Population-level analyses of time-resolved neural recordings show that stimulus decoding is highly time-specific (King and Dehaene, 2014), with discriminative activity patterns changing at the millisecond scale.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior work on dynamic coding.

claim: Dynamic coding has been observed at the level of population spiking patterns within individual brain areas.
source: Such dynamic coding has been observed at the level of population spiking patterns within individual brain areas (Meyers et al., 2008; Crowe et al., 2010; Stokes et al., 2013), and at the level of distributed activation patterns across the cortex (King et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2015), suggesting that this temporal dimension is an inherent aspect of neural coding (Buonomano and Maass, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing multiple prior studies on dynamic coding.

claim: Neural populations in visual and prefrontal cortex appear to represent a memorized stimulus with an independent pattern from that used during initial encoding.
source: Importantly, neural populations in visual (Meyers et al., 2008; Sreenivasan et al., 2014) and prefrontal cortex (Hussar and Pasternak, 2012; 2013; Stokes et al., 2013; Astrand et al., 2015) appear to represent a memorized stimulus with an independent pattern from that used during initial encoding.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing multiple prior studies on memory encoding.

claim: It is necessary to distinguish between a neural pattern (which may vary from moment to moment), and the representational content that is encoded in that pattern (which may be stable even when the pattern changes over time).
source: As a consequence, it is necessary to distinguish between a neural pattern (which may vary from moment to moment), and the representational content that is encoded in that pattern (which may be stable even when the pattern changes over time, see Haxby et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the conceptual distinction between patterns and content, citing prior work.

claim: The highly dynamic trajectory that stimulus processing traces through activation state-space challenges classic models of template representation.
source: The highly dynamic trajectory that stimulus processing traces through activation state-space challenges classic models of template representation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implications of dynamic coding for template models.

claim: Classic models of template representation propose tonic activation of a static neural pattern.
source: These propose tonic activation of a static neural pattern, begging the question: which of the many points along the processing trajectory should be pre-activated?
evidence: This is a direct statement about classic models of template representation.

claim: A matched-filter process could enable templates to guide perceptual decision-making even when stimulus processing is dynamic.
source: An alternative scheme enables templates to guide perceptual decision-making even when stimulus processing is dynamic. If stimulus and template representations rely on different patterns of neural activity in the circuit, then a matched-filter process (c.f. Sugase-Miyamoto et al., 2008; Nikolic et al., 2009; Stokes, 2015) could be envisaged in which the dynamic pattern of stimulus encoding would be automatically transformed into a pattern reflecting the degree of overlap to the template.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an alternative model, citing prior work.

claim: Perceptual decision-making tasks usually require the judgment of a visual stimulus feature against a fixed decision boundary or template.
source: Perceptual decision-making tasks usually require the judgment of a visual stimulus feature against a fixed decision boundary or template (Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about typical perceptual decision-making tasks, citing prior work.

claim: The majority of perceptual decision-making studies have kept the decision boundary (or template) constant over the entire experiment.
source: The majority of perceptual decision-making studies have kept the decision boundary (or template) constant over the entire experiment, impeding a clear evaluation of the representation of templates as distinct from stimulus representation and from the sensory-to-template comparison.
evidence: This is a direct statement about limitations of prior studies.

claim: Neural responses rapidly traversed a cascade of discriminative patterns, transforming the initial task-invariant stimulus code, in conjunction with the template code, into a decision-relevant code.
source: Neural responses rapidly traversed a cascade of discriminative patterns, transforming the initial task-invariant stimulus code, in conjunction with the template code, into a decision-relevant code.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Template patterns and stimulus patterns cross-generalized only in a short time window during initial processing.
source: Template patterns and stimulus patterns cross-generalized only in a short time window during initial processing, suggesting some independence in the two neural codes.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The content of the representation encoded in stimulus and template patterns (as measured by their representational similarity) corresponded over a more sustained period.
source: Despite these differences in the neural patterns, the content of the representation encoded in these patterns (as measured by their representational similarity) corresponded over a more sustained period.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of the main findings.

claim: After the stimulus information was already reliably present and the response-relevant information had begun to emerge, neural signals also encoded the (task-irrelevant) signed difference between the current stimulus and the search template.
source: Interestingly, after the stimulus information was already reliably present and the response-relevant information had begun to emerge, neural signals also encoded the (task-irrelevant) signed difference between the current stimulus and the search template.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The encoding of signed difference is consistent with the use of a population code for perceptual decision-making.
source: We argue, on the basis of a simple neural model, that this effect is consistent with the use of a population code for perceptual decision-making (Ma et al., 2006; Zemel et al., 1998; Beck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the signed difference finding, citing prior work on population codes.

claim: The transient, rather than sustained, activation of template-specific patterns may reflect the reactivation of a latent code that was laid down in altered synaptic weights.
source: The transient, rather than sustained, activation of template-specific patterns may reflect the reactivation of a latent code (Mongillo et al., 2008; Buonomano and Maass, 2009) that was laid down in altered synaptic weights, but which is reactivated via top-down or stimulus-driven input.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an interpretation of the findings, citing prior work.

claim: Template decoding began shortly before stimulus onset, suggesting that the semi-regular timing of events may have allowed for top-down re-activation of the template.
source: Template decoding began shortly before stimulus onset, suggesting that the semi-regular timing of events may have allowed for top-down re-activation of the template (as in 'rhythmic sampling', c.f. Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Lakatos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an interpretation of the findings, citing prior work on rhythmic sampling.

claim: Bottom-up stimulus drive may have additionally activated the template pattern since template decoding peaked during the stimulus presentation period.
source: Since template decoding peaked during the stimulus presentation period, bottom-up stimulus drive may have additionally activated the template pattern.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Matched filters provide a natural solution to the problem of comparing a dynamically evolving stimulus-encoding pattern to a template-encoding pattern.
source: We speculate that matched filters provide a natural solution to the problem of comparing a dynamically evolving stimulus-encoding pattern to a template-encoding pattern: the stimulus pattern is filtered by a population that is matched to the visual characteristics of the template, leading to output that quantifies their overlap.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing a mechanism for template matching.

claim: The task-irrelevant sign of the angular distance was encoded in the MEG/EEG response pattern.
source: Unexpectedly, the task-irrelevant sign of the angular distance was encoded in the MEG/EEG response pattern.
evidence: This is a direct statement about an unexpected finding.

claim: The encoding of the task-irrelevant sign could provide insight into the potential mechanism underlying perceptual decision-making in the task.
source: This finding could provide an interesting insight into the potential mechanism underlying perceptual decision-making in our task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implications of the signed difference finding.

claim: Probabilistic population codes may underlie the representation of the angular distance, and encode the sign of the angular distance as a by-product of decision-making.
source: Specifically, probabilistic population codes may underlie the representation of the angular distance, and encode the sign of the angular distance as a by-product of decision-making.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an interpretation of the signed difference finding.

claim: Stimulus orientation is represented via population codes in early visual cortex.
source: There is evidence that stimulus orientation is represented via population codes in early visual cortex (Graf et al., 2011; Berens et al., 2012), with the activation profile across neurons tuned to many different orientations reflecting a probability distribution peaking at the orientation that is most likely present in the environment.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior work on population coding of orientation.

claim: Mnemonic information (such as a visual template) can be stored through a reconfiguration of synaptic weights, without requiring strong persistent activity.
source: Recent computational and empirical work on the maintenance of items in working memory has argued that mnemonic information (such as a visual template) can be stored through a reconfiguration of synaptic weights (Mongillo et al., 2008; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Stokes et al., 2013), without requiring strong persistent activity (Watanabe and Funahashi, 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior work on working memory mechanisms.

claim: The encoding of decision-relevant mnemonic templates in the weights of a network has the advantage that processing of any new information can immediately pass through the modified weights and produce a matched filter response.
source: The encoding of decision-relevant mnemonic templates in the weights of a network has the crucial advantage that processing of any new information can immediately pass through the modified weights and produce a matched filter response (Mongillo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the advantages of weight-based encoding, citing prior work.

claim: Contents in working memory are decision rules that enforce the current stimulus-response mapping.
source: Conceived in this way, contents in working memory are decision rules that enforce the current stimulus-response mapping (Stokes, 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional role of working memory, citing prior work.

claim: Read-out at the time of the probe consists in a perceptual decision.
source: Read-out at the time of the probe then consists in a perceptual decision (Martínez-García et al., 2011; Pearson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the decision process, citing prior work.

claim: The transient reactivation of the template shortly before stimulus onset could reflect the nature of the task, where the majority of stimuli were non-targets that may have discouraged the use of tonic template activation.
source: The transient reactivation of the template shortly before stimulus onset could also reflect the nature of our task, where the majority of stimuli were non-targets that may have discouraged the use of tonic template activation.
evidence: This is a direct statement proposing an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Single-cell studies have shown that visual distractors presented in a memory delay can disrupt tonic activity of cells coding the remembered item in IT, and transiently in PFC.
source: For instance, single-cell studies have shown that visual distractors presented in a memory delay can disrupt tonic activity of cells coding the remembered item (in IT, Miller et al., 1993, and transiently in PFC, Miller et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior single-cell studies.

claim: Tasks without intervening distractors may be more conducive to the use of tonic activation.
source: By contrast, tasks without intervening distractors may be more conducive to the use of tonic activation (Chelazzi et al., 1993, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing prior work, proposing a task-dependent difference in template activation.

claim: Pattern analysis is a well-established methodology for intracranial multi-unit recordings and for fMRI.
source: While pattern analysis is a well-established methodology for intracranial multi-unit recordings and for fMRI, it is becoming clear that it can provide a useful approach to MEG and EEG as well.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological approach.

claim: Recent modelling demonstrates that the electromagnetic signal contains rich spatiotemporal information suitable for multivariate decoding.
source: Although MEG/EEG measures neural activity at a larger scale relative to micro-electrode recordings, recent modelling demonstrates that the electromagnetic signal contains rich spatiotemporal information suitable for multivariate decoding (Cichy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing recent modeling work on MEG/EEG decoding.

claim: Even subtle differences in dipole position or angle elicit statistically separable patterns at the scalp surface.
source: Even subtle differences in dipole position or angle elicit statistically separable patterns at the scalp surface.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sensitivity of MEG/EEG to subtle neural differences.

claim: For orientation decoding, differences in MEG/EEG patterns presumably depend on idiosyncrasies in the distribution of orientation columns along the cortical surface.
source: For orientation decoding, these differences presumably depend on idiosyncrasies in the distribution of orientation columns along the cortical surface (Cichy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neural basis of orientation decoding, citing prior work.

claim: Decodability does not necessarily imply that the brain is making use of the decodable information.
source: It is important to appreciate that decodability does not necessarily imply that the brain is making use of the decodable information (Tong and Pratte, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of decoding results, citing prior work.

claim: Neural circuits with complex spatiotemporal dynamics could plausibly provide a rich source of information for guiding flexible and context-dependent behavior.
source: Nonetheless, neural circuits with complex spatiotemporal dynamics could plausibly provide a rich source of information for guiding flexible (Miller and Fusi, 2013) and context-dependent behavior (Buonomano and Maass, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional implications of dynamic coding, citing prior work.

claim: The population coding model used is almost identical in architecture and behavior to a more elaborate biophysical model that was recently developed to predict the learning of new categories in lateral intraparietal neurons in monkeys.
source: The population coding model used here is almost identical in architecture and behavior to a more elaborate biophysical model that was recently developed to predict the learning of new categories in a population of lateral intraparietal neurons in monkeys performing an orientation discrimination task (Engel et al., 2015; Freedman and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between the model used and prior biophysical models, citing prior work.

claim: Ethical approval for methods and procedures was obtained from the Central University Research Ethics Committee of the University of Oxford.
source: Ethical approval for methods and procedures was obtained from the Central University Research Ethics Committee of the University of Oxford.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants were paid £10/hr for their time.
source: Ten healthy, right-handed volunteers (age range: 21–27 years, 6 females) took part in the study, and were paid £10/hr for their time.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant compensation.

claim: Visual acuity was normal or corrected to normal.
source: Visual acuity was normal or corrected to normal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Each experimental session lasted approximately 2 hr, of which approximately 1 hr was spent on performing the task.
source: Each participant completed two experimental sessions, approximately 1 week apart, with each lasting approximately 2 hr (of which approximately 1 hr was spent on performing the task).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the duration of experimental sessions.

claim: Stimuli were displayed onto a rear-projection screen placed at a viewing distance of 90 cm.
source: Stimuli were displayed onto a rear-projection screen (placed at a viewing distance of 90 cm) via a projector (Panasonic DLP Projector, PT-D7700E) with a spatial resolution of 1024 × 768 pixels and a refresh rate of 60 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: Gabor patches had a diameter of 4° visual angle and a spatial frequency of 2 cycles/°.
source: The stream consisted of oriented Gabor patches (diameter: 4° visual angle, spatial frequency: 2 cycles/°), presented foveally for 100 ms, at an average rate of 650 ms (inter-stimulus interval, ranging from 516 to 783 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus properties.

claim: Stimuli were presented for 100 ms at an average rate of 650 ms (inter-stimulus interval ranging from 516 to 783 ms).
source: The stream consisted of oriented Gabor patches (diameter: 4° visual angle, spatial frequency: 2 cycles/°), presented foveally for 100 ms, at an average rate of 650 ms (inter-stimulus interval, ranging from 516 to 783 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus timing.

claim: Orientations were drawn without replacement from a set of 16 possible angles, equally spaced from 5.625° to 174.375°, in steps of 11.25°.
source: Orientations were drawn without replacement from a set of 16 possible angles. Stimuli were equally spaced from 5.625° to 174.375°, in steps of 11.25°.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus orientations.

claim: The task consisted of eight brief (approximately 6 min) blocks, in which 480 stimuli were presented (resulting in a total of 3840 stimulus presentations per session).
source: The task consisted of eight brief (approximately 6 min) blocks, in which 480 stimuli were presented (resulting in a total of 3840 stimulus presentations per session).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task structure.

claim: Each block began with the presentation of a target orientation drawn at random, without replacement, from the 16 stimulus orientations.
source: Each block began with the presentation of a target orientation (drawn at random, without replacement, from the 16 stimulus orientations), displayed centrally as a green line (4° length).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task procedure.

claim: Each session contained eight randomly drawn target orientations that did not need to repeat across experimental sessions.
source: Thus, each session contained eight randomly drawn target orientations (they did not need to repeat across experimental sessions).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the target selection procedure.

claim: Since stimuli were drawn equiprobably from the 16 possible orientations, 1/16 of all stimuli were targets.
source: Since stimuli were drawn equiprobably from the 16 possible orientations, 1/16 of all stimuli were targets.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the target frequency.

claim: All data and fully annotated analysis scripts from this study are publicly available.
source: In accordance with the principles of open evaluation in science (Walther and van den Bosch, 2012), all data and fully annotated analysis scripts from this study are publicly available at http://datasharedrive.blogspot.co.uk/2015/08/testing-sensory-evidence-against.html (see also Myers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Neuromagnetic data were acquired using a whole-head VectorView system with 204 planar gradiometers and 102 magnetometers.
source: Neuromagnetic data were acquired using a whole-head VectorView system (204 planar gradiometers, 102 magnetometers, Elekta Neuromag Oy, Helsinki, Finland).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MEG acquisition system.

claim: Magnetoencephalographic signals were sampled at a rate of 1,000 Hz and on-line band-pass filtered between 0.03 and 300 Hz.
source: Magnetoencephalographic signals were sampled at a rate of 1,000 Hz and on-line band-pass filtered between 0.03 and 300 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MEG acquisition parameters.

claim: EEG data were collected in half of the sessions using 60 channels distributed across the scalp via the international 10–10 positioning system.
source: EEG data were collected in half of the sessions (for each participant), using 60 channels distributed across the scalp via the international 10–10 positioning system (AEEGS, 1991).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition.

claim: Data were preprocessed using the in-house OHBA software library, drawing on SPM8, Fieldtrip, and Elekta software.
source: Data were preprocessed using the in-house OHBA software library (OSL), drawing on SPM8 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm), Fieldtrip (Oostenveld et al., 2011), and Elekta software.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the preprocessing software.

claim: The raw MEG data were de-noised and motion-corrected using Maxfilter Signal Space Separation.
source: The raw MEG data were visually inspected to remove and interpolate any channels with excessive noise, and were further de-noised and motion-corrected using Maxfilter Signal Space Separation (Taulu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the preprocessing steps, citing the method.

claim: Data were downsampled to 500 Hz.
source: Next, data were downsampled to 500 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the preprocessing steps.

claim: Systematic artefacts, arising from eye blinks and heart beats, were identified via independent component analysis, and regressed out of the raw data.
source: Systematic artefacts, arising from eye blinks and heart beats, were identified via independent component analysis, and regressed out of the raw data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the artifact removal procedure.

claim: Data were epoched from –1 to + 1 s with respect to each stimulus onset.
source: The cleaned data were then epoched with respect to each stimulus onset (from –1 to + 1 s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the epoching procedure.

claim: All data were baseline-corrected by subtracting the mean signal between –150 and –50 ms relative to stimulus onset.
source: All data were then baseline-corrected by subtracting the mean signal between –150 and –50 ms relative to stimulus onset (for analyses relating to the template, we used an earlier baseline, from –200 to –150 ms relative to stimulus onset, to explore the possibility that template information might be 'pre-activated' around the expected onset time. Using the standard baseline from –150 to –50 ms, however, did not change the results presented here).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the baseline correction procedure.

claim: A population tuning curve model was used to recover information about the stimulus orientation from the full M/EEG signal.
source: We used a population tuning curve model to recover information about the stimulus orientation from the full M/EEG signal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the decoding method.

claim: Tuning curve models are well suited to recovering information about parametric features like orientations or colors.
source: Tuning curve models are well suited to recovering information about parametric features like orientations (Saproo and Serences, 2010; Brouwer and Heeger, 2011; Serences and Saproo, 2012; Garcia et al., 2013) or colors (Brouwer and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the suitability of tuning curve models, citing prior work.

claim: Data were separated into a training set (all trials from 7 of 8 blocks) and a test set (the left-out block).
source: To recover stimulus orientations, data were separated into a training set (all trials from 7 of 8 blocks) and a test set (the left-out block).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cross-validation procedure.

claim: The regressor matrix was convolved with a half-cosine basis set raised to the 15th power.
source: The regressor matrix was then convolved with a half-cosine basis set (raised to the 15th power, see Brouwer and Heeger, 2009), in order to pool information across similar orientations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the basis set used for decoding, citing prior work.

claim: Orientation sensitivity at each MEG/EEG sensor was calculated by regressing the design matrix against the signal, separately for all time points in the epoch.
source: Orientation sensitivity at each MEG/EEG sensor was then calculated by regressing the design matrix against the signal (across all 306 sensors or all 366 sensors in MEG+EEG sessions), separately for all time points in the epoch (in 4 ms steps, using a sliding window of 20 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the regression procedure.

claim: Multiple comparisons across time were corrected for using cluster-based permutation testing with 10,000 permutations.
source: Multiple comparisons across time were corrected for using cluster-based permutation testing (10,000 permutations, Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the multiple comparisons correction method, citing prior work.

claim: Onset latencies between stimulus, template, and angular distance were compared using a jack-knife approach.
source: Onset latencies between stimulus, template, and angular distance were compared using a jack-knife approach (Miller, Patterson and Ulrich, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the latency comparison method, citing prior work.

claim: The baseline-corrected signal at each sensor and time point was fit using a general linear model consisting of pairs of regressors containing the sine and cosine of the three task orientations, along with a constant regressor.
source: The baseline-corrected signal at each sensor and time point in the epoch was fit (across all trials) using a general linear model (GLM) consisting of pairs of regressors containing the sine and cosine of the three task orientations, along with a constant regressor.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the univariate sensitivity analysis method.

claim: The observed amplitude was ranked within the permutation distribution of amplitudes to calculate a p-value, which was transformed into a z score.
source: The observed (unpermuted) amplitude was ranked within the permutation distribution of amplitudes to calculate a p-value, which was transformed into a z score using the inverse of the cumulative Gaussian distribution (with center 0 and standard deviation 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical testing procedure.

claim: Dynamic coding can be inferred by comparing the decoding slopes on within-time training with the decoding slopes on between-time training.
source: Dynamic coding can be inferred by comparing the decoding slopes on within-time training (i.e., training and testing on time t1, or time t2) with the decoding slopes on between-time training (i.e., training on t1 and testing on t2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the criterion for dynamic coding.

claim: The criterion for a dynamic epoch was: for each pair of time points ti,j, coding is dynamic if the tuning curve slope is significantly higher within time than across time (ti,i > ti,j AND tj,j > ti,j).
source: Our criterion for a dynamic epoch was: for each pair of time points ti,j, coding is dynamic if the tuning curve slope is significantly higher (as measured by a paired t-test across 10 participants) within time than across time (ti,i > ti,j AND tj,j > ti,j).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical criterion for dynamic coding.

claim: Dissimilarity was quantified by the Mahalanobis distance matrices between all pairs of stimulus orientations.
source: Dissimilarity was quantified by the Mahalanobis distance matrices between all pairs of stimulus orientations (on one half of trials), separately for each time point in the trial.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dissimilarity metric used in RSA.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between distance matrices from two independent data sets, for each combination of time points.
source: We next calculated the same distance matrix for the remaining half of the data, and calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between distance matrices from the two independent data sets, for each combination of time points.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the RSA correlation procedure.

claim: Data dimensionality was reduced from 306 sensors (or 306+60 sensors for MEG+EEG sessions) to 30 principal components.
source: First, in order to de-noise the data, we smoothed data with a 20-ms Gaussian kernel and reduced the dimensionality of the MEG signal from 306 sensors (or 306+60 sensors for MEG+EEG sessions) to 30 principal components (PCs) by calculating coefficients over the average time series at each sensor.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dimensionality reduction procedure.

claim: The regressors were derived from the three main task variables: stimulus orientation, template orientation, and angular distance.
source: The regressors were derived from the three main task variables: stimulus orientation, template orientation, and angular distance.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task variables used in the angular distance analysis.

claim: Since all three task variables are circular variables, pairs of regressors consisting of the sine and cosine of each task angle were used, yielding a design matrix consisting of six regressors in total.
source: Since all three are circular variables, we used pairs of regressors, consisting of the sine and cosine of each task angle, yielding a design matrix consisting of six regressors in total.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the regressor design for circular variables.

claim: The GLM was solved on normalized data by subtracting the mean and dividing by the variance across all trials in the training set.
source: The GLM was solved on normalized data (by subtracting the mean and dividing by the variance across all trials in the training set).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data normalization procedure.

claim: The regression coefficients were symmetrically orthogonalized following Mante et al., 2013.
source: This yielded a set of six regression coefficients ('betas') for each time point in the trial and for each of the 30 PCs, which were then symmetrically orthogonalized (Colclough et al., 2015; following Mante et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthogonalization procedure, citing prior work.

claim: The cosine regressor for angular distance measured only the task-relevant aspect of the angle (i.e., the decision value).
source: In particular, the two regressors for the angular distance partialled out task-relevant and task-irrelevant aspects of the angular distance between stimulus and template: the cosine regressor, with a maximum of 1 at 0º (targets), a minimum of –1 at the farthest non-targets ( ± 90º, in our 180º orientation space), and equal magnitudes for equivalent non-targets (e.g., 0.92 for both +11º and –11º), measured only the task-relevant aspect of the angle (i.e., the decision value, as shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the cosine regressor.

claim: The sine regressor is insensitive to decision value but distinguished between signed differences between non-targets.
source: By contrast, the sine regressor is insensitive to decision value (since, in 180º orientation space, sin(0º) = sin( ± 90º) = 0), but distinguished between signed differences between non-targets (e.g., sin(+11º) = 0.38 = −sin(–11º)).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the sine regressor.

claim: The model consisted of a three-layer architecture, with each layer encoding information about one of the three task variables (stimulus, template, and angular distance).
source: The model consisted of a three-layer architecture, with each layer consisting of neurons coding for different task variables (a stimulus layer, a template layer, and a decision layer).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the neural model architecture.

claim: The stimulus layer consisted of 100 units, each tuned to a different veridical stimulus orientation, with tuning determined by a von Mises distribution.
source: The stimulus layer consisted of a set of 100 units, each tuned to a different veridical stimulus orientation, with tuning determined by a von Mises distribution
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus layer of the model.

claim: In the stimulus layer, the concentration parameter was set to 5.
source: In the stimulus layer, the concentration parameter was set to 5 (see Beck et al., 2008, for the same parameter choice).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model parameter, citing prior work.

claim: The template layer was identical to the stimulus layer, with the exception that template tuning was broader (κ = 2).
source: The template layer was identical to the stimulus layer, with the exception that template tuning was broader (κ = 2), under the assumption that remembered stimuli would be encoded with lower precision than currently visible stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the template layer of the model.

claim: The decision layer was identical to the template layer, with the conceptual difference that units were tuned to decision-relative orientations rather than veridical stimulus orientations.
source: Finally, the decision layer was identical to the template layer, with the conceptual difference that here, units were not tuned to veridical stimulus orientations, but to decision-relative orientations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the decision layer of the model.

claim: The stimulus and template layers were connected via a one-to-one mapping between identically tuned units.
source: The stimulus and template layers were connected via a one-to-one mapping between identically tuned units (weight matrix WST, with all connections between non-identical orientations set to 0).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the connectivity in the model.

claim: Activation in the template layer was updated as a function of activation in the stimulus layer by computing the element-wise product between RS and RT.
source: In a second step, corresponding to a later processing stage, activation in the template layer was updated as a function of activation in the stimulus layer, by computing the element-wise product between RS and RT.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the computation in the model.

claim: This step is similar to a Bayesian update, in which the prior distribution (the template layer response) is multiplied with the current evidence (the stimulus layer response) to produce a posterior distribution.
source: This step is similar to a Bayesian update, in which the prior distribution (the template layer response) is multiplied with the current evidence (the stimulus layer response) to produce a posterior distribution.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the model computation.

claim: The crucial mapping for the task was between the template and decision layers, which consisted of an all-to-all reciprocal weight matrix WTD.
source: The crucial mapping for the task was between the template and decision layers, which consisted of an all-to-all reciprocal weight matrix WTD.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the key connectivity in the model.

claim: Only the weight matrix WTD needs to change in response to a change in the current template orientation.
source: Importantly, only the weight matrix WTD needs to change in response to a change in the current template orientation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the flexibility of the model.
